# Electrical facts guide (DRAFT)

The well-established US facts an electrical script may use when the brief is silent: code rules, safety facts, standard sizes and settings, and every step for the dangerous situations. This channel uses no money at all, so this guide takes the place the price guide holds in the plumbing pack. Drafted 2026-10-27 by one researcher, from primary and code-focused sources (CPSC, CDC, OSHA tables, NFPA, IAEI, EC&M, Mike Holt, manufacturers' instruction sheets, utilities) plus the three source-checked brief rounds in `niche-research/studies/electrical/ideation/briefs-work/` (check-c1, check-c2, check-c3), then re-checked row by row by a second researcher (below). Code facts are from the 2023 National Electrical Code (NEC) as summarized by code-focused publishers; nobody read the NFPA 70 text itself. Re-check the guide when a new NEC edition is adopted (the 2026 NEC is out) and at least once a year.

**Re-check (2026-10-27):** a second researcher re-checked 214 of the 228 rows in sections 1 to 13: every row marked one source or reading, every safety row (sections 8, 9, 11 and 12, and every shock, fire, generator, panel, GFCI and AFCI row elsewhere) and a sample of 33 confirmed rows from sections 1 to 7 and 10, each against a source other than the one first cited where one could be found (OSHA 3075 read directly, MedlinePlus, Ready.gov, CPSC's current CO pages, USFA, a utility, Mike Holt's 2023 code-change books, a city NM-cable guide, Leviton, Lutron, Fluke, Wago, Southwire, InterNACHI, NAHB). Rows that say what a named source says (CPSC, DOE, a maker) were re-read against that source's own text. All 49 glossary entries were read for correctness and plainness. Result: 165 confirmed, 35 adjusted, 9 thin, 5 kept on their cited sources with no new one found; 5 glossary entries corrected. No prices found. Every row checked, with before, after and source, is in `studies/electrical/facts-research-2026-10-27/recheck.md`.

## How to use it

- **The brief comes first.** Use this guide only for a fact the brief doesn't give. Where the brief and the guide disagree on safety, the safer one wins and the disagreement is flagged.
- **No money, ever.** No prices, costs, savings, bills or "a cheap fix". If a row seems to need a cost, it doesn't belong in a script.
- **Code is local.** The NEC is a model code; each state or town adopts an edition (some are a cycle or two behind) and amends it, and the local inspector has the final say (row 13.1). Say a code rule as "the national electrical code", "the code in most places" or "newer code", and add "check with your local inspector" wherever the local rule decides. Never say a viewer's older house "is illegal": most rules apply to new work and replacements, not to what's already there.
- **Article numbers stay off the air** unless the brief uses them. The NEC column is for the scanner and the evidence block. (Operator call: see the note at the end.)
- **Name the source only where it helps,** and only when the row says "can cite": the Consumer Product Safety Commission, the CDC, OSHA and the National Fire Protection Association carry weight with this audience. When the script names a source, say its figure as the source gives it.
- **Status** column: **confirmed** (two independent sources agree), **one source** (usable, said plainly but without extra certainty; say "generally", "usually" or attribute it), **reading** (this researcher's interpretation or general trade knowledge not checked against a source this round: say it in general words or leave it out). After the re-check: **confirmed (re-checked)** (a second source agrees), **adjusted (re-checked)** (the fact was corrected; the row shows the corrected version and what changed), **thin** (the second researcher couldn't verify it: keep it out of scripts), **confirmed (kept)** (no new source found; the first two sources stand). A clause marked reading inside a confirmed row stays reading.
- **The dangerous situations get every step,** whatever the brief leaves out, in the script's own words: someone being shocked (12.8 to 12.11), a hot outlet or burning smell (12.13 to 12.15), a downed line (12.12), generator carbon monoxide (11.1 to 11.7) and backfeeding (11.8 to 11.12). Same rule as the gas-leak row in the plumbing pack.
- **Verify dead, every time.** Any step that opens a box, a fixture or a device says, in one line, breaker off and verified dead with a tester (8.1, 8.2). Anything inside the panel is an electrician's job (9.4).

Never say "a 20-amp breaker makes the circuit stronger": the wire decides the breaker.

## 6. GFCI and AFCI behaviour

| # | Fact | Source | NEC 2023 | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | A GFCI compares the current going out on the hot wire with the current coming back on the neutral; if some is leaking away (possibly through a person), it shuts off. | ESFI in IAEI, https://iaeimagazine.org/electrical-safety/ground-fault-circuit-interrupters-preventing-electrocution-since-1971/ ; Mike Holt, https://www.mikeholt.com/files/PDF/23UNEC1_210.8.pdf ; re-check: OSHA 3075, Controlling Electrical Hazards; InterNACHI GFCIs | Art. 100 (GFCI) | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.2 | A household (Class A) GFCI trips when about 6 thousandths of an amp (6 milliamps) leaks, and won't trip below 4. | IAEI, https://iaeimagazine.org/issue/2024-summer/the-history-of-gfci-protection-in-the-nec/ ; Mike Holt forum, https://forums.mikeholt.com/goto/post?id=1065519 ; re-check: InterNACHI GFCIs | Art. 100 | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.3 | A regular breaker doesn't protect people: the smallest household breaker needs about 15,000 milliamps to trip, and a tenth of that can stop a heart (see 12.3). That's the GFCI's job. | CPWR student manual, https://elcosh.org/document/1624/888/d000543/section2.html ; OSHAcademy, https://www.oshacademy.com/courses/training/809-focus-four-electrocution-hazards/809-1-5.php ; re-check: OSHA 3075, Controlling Electrical Hazards; TUV Rheinland current-effects sheet | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.4 | A GFCI does not protect against overloads, short circuits, or a shock from touching the hot and neutral wires at once while standing on something that doesn't conduct (Leviton). Power still goes off before work. | Leviton GFCI instructions, https://leviton.com/content/dam/leviton/residential/product_documents/instruction_sheet/GFNL1-GFNL2_Instruction_Sheet_English.pdf ; re-check: OSHA 3075, Controlling Electrical Hazards | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.5 | Test every GFCI once a month: plug in a lamp, press TEST and the lamp goes out, press RESET and it comes back. If it doesn't, replace the GFCI (CPSC: can cite). | CPSC Pub. 513, https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/513.pdf ; Leviton GFCI instructions (same as 6.4) ; re-check: InterNACHI GFCIs | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.6 | GFCI and AFCI breakers get tested monthly too: press the test button and the handle should move to the middle or off; reset by pushing it fully off, then on. A bad one is replaced by a qualified electrician. | CPSC Pub. 513, https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/513.pdf ; re-check: ESFI How to Test an AFCI (search summary) and Siemens AFCI FAQ quoted on Mike Holt forum | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.7 | GFCIs and AFCIs can fail without any sign, which is why the monthly test matters (CPSC). | CPSC Pub. 513, https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/513.pdf ; re-check: CPSC publication text re-read word for word (513, 516, 518, 5032; copies in this folder); ESFI How to Test an AFCI (search summary) and Siemens AFCI FAQ quoted on Mike Holt forum | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.8 | GFCI receptacles made since June 29, 2015 test themselves (at least every three hours under UL 943); when one fails, it shuts off power and won't reset, or keeps tripping. | IAEI UL Question Corner, https://iaeimagazine.org/magazine/columns/ul-question-corner/ul-question-corner-self-testing-gfci-requirements/ ; HD Supply, https://www.hdsupplysolutions.com/s/gfci_receptacles_legislation ; re-check: Leviton GFNL1 sheet (re-read, self-test section) | none (UL 943) | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.9 | On a self-testing Leviton GFCI, a solid or flashing red light means a problem; if it won't reset after TEST, replace it. | Leviton GFCI instructions (same as 6.4) ; re-check: Leviton GFNL1 sheet (re-read, self-test section) | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.10 | LINE terminals take the power coming from the panel; LOAD terminals feed the outlets beyond it, which are then protected too, even in another room, and have no buttons of their own. | Leviton GFCI instructions (same as 6.4); HomeTips, https://www.hometips.com/repair-fix/outlet-has-no-power-but-breaker-not-tripped.html (checked brief C15) ; re-check: Mike Holt, Understanding the 2023 NEC, 210.8 extract (re-read) | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 6.11 | A modern GFCI won't reset if no power reaches it (a tripped breaker, a loose connection upstream), if LINE and LOAD were swapped, or if it has reached end of life. | Leviton GFCI instructions (same as 6.4); Leviton blog, https://leviton.com/support/literature/blogs/leviton-s-reset-lockout-technology--the-safety-upgrade-that-gfci ; re-check: InterNACHI GFCIs; Leviton GFNL1 sheet (re-read, self-test section) | none | confirmed (re-checked) |

Never give a GFCI trip time ("a fortieth of a second") as a rule: UL sets a curve, and that figure is one maker's spec.

## 8. Testers and how to verify dead

| # | Fact | Source | NEC 2023 | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.1 | Before touching any wire: breaker off, then test that the power is actually off. Every maker's instructions say both. | Leviton AC215/AC220 sheet, https://inspectapedia.com/electric/Duplex-receptacle-install-instructions-Leviton.pdf ; Leviton GFCI instructions, https://leviton.com/content/dam/leviton/residential/product_documents/instruction_sheet/GFNL1-GFNL2_Instruction_Sheet_English.pdf ; re-check: Leviton 05503 three-way switch sheet; Leviton 5243 three-way switch sheet | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.2 | The three-point test (live, dead, live): check the tester on an outlet you know is live, test the wires you'll touch, then check the tester on the live outlet again. A dead battery can't fool you that way. | NFPA 70E summary, https://www.graceport.com/blog/what-is-an-absence-of-voltage-test-nfpa-70e-requirements-explained ; Mike Holt forum (Klein), https://forums.mikeholt.com/threads/non-contact-voltage-detector-less-than-100-effective.2572887 (checked brief A33) ; re-check: Reliable Plant on absence-of-voltage testing, and Mike Holt forum | NFPA 70E 110.6(E), 120.5 | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.3 | A non-contact pen tester can stay silent on a live wire: inside a metal box, on shielded or armored cable, with a weak battery, or when you're well insulated from ground. It can also beep falsely. Silence never proves a wire is dead. | Fluke, https://www.fluke.com/en-ca/learn/blog/electrical/best-electrical-voltage-testers ; Mike Holt forum (same as 8.2) ; re-check: Fluke blog page explaining the capacitive (non-contact) sensor; Reliable Plant on absence-of-voltage testing, and Mike Holt forum | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.4 | Workplace practice under NFPA 70E treats a non-contact tester as a first check only: proving a circuit dead takes a two-probe tester or meter on every wire, hot to neutral, hot to ground and neutral to ground. | Graceport (same as 8.2); Mike Holt forum, https://forums.mikeholt.com/threads/verifying-no-voltage-prior-to-work.105149/latest ; re-check: Reliable Plant on absence-of-voltage testing, and Mike Holt forum | NFPA 70E 120.5 | adjusted (re-checked): softened to what sources say |
| 8.5 | Test every wire in the box, not just the one you're working on: one box can hold more than one circuit, and a split receptacle can be on two breakers (4.27). | checked brief C12; reading ; re-check: Reliable Plant on absence-of-voltage testing, and Mike Holt forum; Leviton 05503 three-way switch sheet | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.6 | A shared-neutral (multiwire) circuit runs two hots on one neutral, and the two breakers must be tied together or be a two-pole breaker so both go off together. With one side still on, that neutral can carry current. | Mike Holt forum, https://forums.mikeholt.com/goto/post?id=1294111 ; EC&M, https://www.ecmweb.com/national-electrical-code/article/20887244/code-qa ; re-check: Mike Holt, Summary of the 2023 Changes to the NEC | 210.4(B) | confirmed (re-checked; neutral-current clause rests on the neutral definition (14.2)) |
| 8.7 | A meter on a working 120-volt outlet, set to AC volts: about 120 hot to neutral (anywhere from about 110 to 125), about the same hot to ground, and close to zero neutral to ground. The short slot is the hot. | Fluke, https://fluke.com/en-us/learn/blog/electrical/troubleshooting-electrical-outlets-in-residential-applications ; EngineerFix, https://engineerfix.com/how-to-test-outlet-voltage-with-a-multimeter/ | none | confirmed (kept: cited sources stand; no new source this round) |
| 8.8 | On a 240-volt circuit, a meter reads about 240 between the two hots and about 120 from either hot to neutral or ground. | follows from 1.15 ; re-check: Eversource backfeed page (re-read) | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.9 | For household outlets and panels, use a meter rated CAT III 600 volts or better; the rating is printed by the jacks. | Fluke (same as 8.3); FMLink on Fluke 114-117, https://www.fmlink.com/flukes-new-family-of-dmms-determines-proper-grounding-with-visual-indicator/ ; re-check: Fluke, How to Choose the Correct Fuse for Your Tester | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.10 | Leads go in the volts jacks for voltage, never the amps jack; a meter left on amps and touched across an outlet is a dead short in your hand. | general trade knowledge; not checked this round ; re-check: Fluke, How to Choose the Correct Fuse for Your Tester | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.11 | A three-light plug-in tester shows an open ground, reversed polarity and some open wires, but it can't detect a bootleg ground and can be fooled. It's a check, never permission to touch. | JLC, https://www.jlconline.com/how-to/electrical/plug-in-electrical-testers_o/ ; EC&M, https://www.ecmweb.com/construction/article/20897728/failures-in-outlet-testing-exposed ; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_outlet_tester | none | confirmed (kept: cited sources stand; no new source this round) |
| 8.12 | A clamp meter reads current around one wire; clamped around a whole cord it reads nearly zero. | general trade knowledge; not checked this round | none | thin (re-checked): no source found; keep out of scripts |
| 8.13 | At home, tape over the breaker you switched off and leave a note, so nobody flips it back on while you work. | reading (workplaces use formal lockout, OSHA 1910.147) ; re-check: OSHA 3075, Controlling Electrical Hazards | none | confirmed (re-checked) |
| 8.14 | Breaker labels can be wrong. Trust the tester, not the panel directory. | reading ; re-check: Leviton 05503 three-way switch sheet; Leviton 5243 three-way switch sheet | none | confirmed (re-checked) |

Testing is the only live work a script ever describes: a tester's probes in the outlet slots, or on wires before anyone touches them, holding the tester by its insulated grips. Never touch a wire, terminal or box to check for power, and never test with the panel's dead-front off.

## 14. Terms to explain the first time

One clause each, in plain words. The script explains each the first time it's used.

| # | Term | Plain explanation | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14.1 | Hot wire | the wire that carries the power from the breaker, usually black or red | CPSC Pub. 518; Leviton sheets (4.19) | confirmed |
| 14.2 | Neutral | the white wire that carries the current back to the panel; it's connected to the earth at the main panel, but it carries current and can shock you | EC&M definitions, https://www.ecmweb.com/national-electrical-code/article/20889345/grounding-bonding-definitions ; checked brief A29 | confirmed |
| 14.3 | Ground (grounding wire) | the bare or green wire that gives stray current a safe path back so the breaker trips; normally it carries nothing | EC&M definitions (same as 14.2) | one source |
| 14.4 | Bonding | connecting all the metal parts together so they can't be at different voltages | EC&M definitions (same as 14.2) | one source |
| 14.5 | Main bonding jumper | the one place, in the main panel, where neutral and ground are joined | Mike Holt forum (9.13) | one source |
| 14.6 | Volt | the electrical "pressure" pushing the current | general knowledge | reading |
| 14.7 | Amp | how much current is flowing | general knowledge | reading |
| 14.8 | Watt | how much power is being used: volts times amps | Mike Holt forum (1.10) | confirmed |
| 14.9 | Circuit | one breaker and everything it feeds | general knowledge | reading |
| 14.10 | AWG (wire gauge) | the wire's size; the smaller the number, the thicker the wire | CPSC Pub. 5032 | one source |
| 14.11 | NM cable, "Romex" | the plastic-jacketed cable inside most house walls; Romex is Southwire's brand name for it | CPSC Pub. 516 ("NM, often called Romex"); checked brief B10 | confirmed |
| 14.12 | UF cable | a tougher cable made for wet places and burial in the ground | checked brief B10 | one source |
| 14.13 | Breaker | an automatic switch that shuts a circuit off when too much current flows, to protect the wire | checked brief A33 | reading |
| 14.14 | Fuse | the older one-time version of a breaker: a strip inside melts to stop the current | general knowledge | reading |
| 14.15 | Overload | more current than the wire is meant to carry, usually too many things on one circuit | CPSC Pub. 5032 | reading |
| 14.16 | Short circuit | the hot touching neutral or ground directly, a sudden rush of current | general knowledge | reading |
| 14.17 | Ground fault | current leaking out of the circuit through something it shouldn't, such as water, metal or a person | ESFI in IAEI (6.1) | one source |
| 14.18 | Arc | electricity jumping a gap, as at a loose connection or damaged wire; it's very hot | CPSC Pub. 513 (AFCI answer) | one source |
| 14.19 | GFCI (ground-fault circuit interrupter) | an outlet with TEST and RESET buttons, or a breaker with a TEST button, that shuts off in a split second if current leaks, to protect people from shock | Mike Holt (Art. 100), https://www.mikeholt.com/files/PDF/23UNEC1_210.8.pdf ; IAEI (6.2) | adjusted (re-checked): a GFCI breaker has a TEST button but no RESET button |
| 14.20 | AFCI (arc-fault circuit interrupter) | a breaker or outlet that shuts off when it senses dangerous arcing, to prevent fires | CPSC Pub. 513; NFPA checklist | confirmed |
| 14.21 | Dual-function | one breaker or outlet that does the GFCI and AFCI jobs together | checked brief C15 | one source |
| 14.22 | Line and load | on a GFCI, LINE is where the power comes in and LOAD is where it goes on to other outlets | Leviton GFCI instructions | one source |
| 14.23 | Tamper-resistant (TR) | an outlet with built-in shutters so a child can't push something into one slot | EC&M Magazine (4.1); InterNACHI (4.1) | confirmed |
| 14.24 | Weather-resistant (WR) | an outlet built to stand up to outdoor damp and cold | Leviton (4.3) | one source |
| 14.25 | Polarized plug | a plug with one wider blade so it only goes in one way | CPSC Pub. 518 | one source |
| 14.26 | Pigtail | a short piece of wire that joins the wires in the box to the device, so only one wire goes on each screw | checked briefs A2, C2 | one source |
| 14.27 | Backstab (push-in) | the small holes in the back of many outlets where a wire is just pushed in and held by a spring | IAEI (3.6) | adjusted (re-checked): "cheap outlets" was wrong: push-in holes are on many outlets |
| 14.28 | Wire nut | a twist-on cap, usually with a metal spring inside, that joins wires | Ideal (3.11) | adjusted (re-checked): not every wire nut has a spring |
| 14.29 | Lever connector (Wago) | a connector, often clear, with little levers that clamp each wire | Wago (3.13) | adjusted (re-checked): not every lever connector is clear |
| 14.30 | Box fill | how many wires and devices a box is big enough to hold | EC&M (2.1) | one source |
| 14.31 | Double tap | two wires under a breaker screw made for one | checked brief A30 | one source |
| 14.32 | Dead-front | the inner metal cover of the panel that hides the live parts; it comes off only for an electrician | reading | reading |
| 14.33 | Service panel, subpanel | the main breaker box where power enters the house; a subpanel is a second, smaller one fed from it | general knowledge | reading |
| 14.34 | Multiwire (shared-neutral) circuit | two circuits sharing one neutral wire, with their breakers tied together | Mike Holt forum (8.6) | one source |
| 14.35 | Bootleg ground | a jumper from neutral to the ground screw that fakes a ground; against code | Mike Holt forum; Wikipedia (7.11) | confirmed |
| 14.36 | CO/ALR | the marking on a switch or outlet rated for aluminum wire | CPSC Pub. 516 | one source |
| 14.37 | Knob-and-tube | the oldest house wiring: single wires on porcelain knobs, no ground | InterNACHI (7.1) | one source |
| 14.38 | Continuous load | anything that runs three hours or more, such as an EV charger | Mike Holt forum; EC&M (1.11) | confirmed |
| 14.39 | Level 1, Level 2 charging | Level 1 is an ordinary 120-volt outlet; Level 2 is a 240-volt circuit like a dryer's | US DOE AFDC (10.5) | one source |
| 14.40 | Interlock | a sliding plate on the panel that lets the main breaker or the generator breaker be on, never both | IAEI (11.15); checked brief A7 | confirmed |
| 14.41 | Transfer switch | a separate switch panel that moves chosen circuits from the utility to the generator, so the two can never connect | Eversource (11.8); checked brief A7 | confirmed |
| 14.42 | Power inlet (inlet box) | an outdoor socket on the house wall with recessed prongs, where the generator cord plugs in | checked briefs A7, B11 | one source |
| 14.43 | Backfeed | sending generator power backwards into the house wiring, and out to the street, through an outlet | CPSC Alert; Eversource (11.8) | confirmed |
| 14.44 | Bonded, floating neutral | whether the generator's neutral is tied to its frame (bonded) or not (floating) | Generac (11.19) | one source |
| 14.45 | Carbon monoxide (CO) | the invisible, odorless poison in engine exhaust | CPSC Alert; CDC (11.1) | confirmed |
| 14.46 | Non-contact voltage tester | the pen-shaped tester that beeps near a live wire without touching it; it can miss a live wire (8.3) | Fluke (8.3) | adjusted (re-checked): added the warning, so the term is never explained as proof of dead |
| 14.47 | Multimeter | a meter with two probes that reads the actual voltage | general knowledge | reading |
| 14.48 | Listed, UL listed | tested and certified by a lab such as UL, ETL (Intertek) or CSA | CPSC Pub. 5032 | one source |
| 14.49 | Inspector, AHJ | the local official who enforces the electrical code and has the final say | IAEI (13.1) | one source |
| 14.50 | Open ground (on a plug-in tester) | the light pattern that means no ground wire is connected at that outlet; the missing wire causes it, not a GFCI | plug-in tester labels (general knowledge); 4.17 | reading |
